titleDv: ޤާނޫނު ނަންބަރު 12/2016 (ޖިނާއީ އިޖުރާއަތުގެ ޤާނޫނު) އަށް ... ވަނަ އިޞްލާޙު ގެނައުމުގެ ބިލު
summary: This government bill amends the Criminal Procedure Act (Law No. 12/2016). Its explanatory note says it gives police procedures for investigating cybercrime and collecting electronic evidence. These include getting subscriber and traffic data from service providers, quickly preserving computer data, production orders, searching and seizing computer data, and collecting traffic data or intercepting content in real time. The pages read mostly deal with detention and release: they change the grounds for keeping a suspect in custody (Article 60), rewrite Article 61, add new Articles 61-1 and 66-1, and amend Articles 62, 65 and 68. They also rewrite Article 74 so police can use special surveillance, with a court order, when investigating a listed set of serious crimes. This summary covers the first 12 of 70 pages, and the scans are hard to read, so some details are uncertain.
whyItMatters: It would affect when suspects can be kept in custody or released before and during trial, and let police monitor people's communications and computer data in serious and cyber crime investigations.
keyProvisions: Article 60(h)(4) is rewritten so that a reasonable belief that the person may commit another offence, or may endanger public safety, is a ground for keeping them in custody.

Article 61 is rewritten and a new Article 61-1 is added on releasing suspects. The court must weigh listed factors, including the person's criminal record, whether they might interfere with witnesses or evidence, and whether they might flee. The exact wording is hard to read.
New subsections are added to Articles 62 and 65, and Article 68(h) is rewritten. Together they deal with decisions to keep or release people under Articles 64, 65, 66 and 66-1.
A new Article 66-1 covers keeping or releasing an accused person while their trial is ongoing, with a reference to Article 160 of the law. Details could not be read reliably.

Article 74 is rewritten so police can use special surveillance under a court order when investigating murder, organised serious crime, terrorism, money laundering and terrorist financing, human trafficking, drug trafficking, child sexual abuse and offences under Article 246 of the Penal Code. Another listed category appears to cover corruption-related offences, but it is hard to read.

The explanatory note lists further cybercrime investigation powers, such as service-provider data requests, preserving computer data, production orders, search and seizure of computer data, and real-time collection or interception. The clauses for these come after the pages read.
whoIsAffected: People arrested or charged with crimes, courts and police, and telecom and internet service providers asked to hand over or preserve data.
statedReasons: The government says cybercrime is increasing and the current law does not give investigators the powers needed to investigate it and collect electronic evidence, so it is amending Law 12/2016. It also proposes changes about detention and court procedure.
